name: Sasanian Empire
summary: The last pre-Islamic Persian empire and Rome’s great rival for four centuries, ended by the Arab conquests.

location.value: Iran, Iraq and parts of Arabia, the Caucasus, the Levant, Central Asia and northwestern India, ruled from Ctesiphon.

terrain.value: The Iranian plateau and the Mesopotamian river plain.

climate.value: Arid to semi-arid, with irrigation in Mesopotamia.

resources.value: Mesopotamian agriculture, silk-road trade and silver.

disasters.value: The Plague of Justinian (from 541) also struck Persia. A plague in 627–628 contributed to instability.

population.value: Not given in the Wikipedia infobox.

urbanisation.value: Ctesiphon (capital, 226–637) was one of the largest cities in the world. Many royal cities were founded.

migration.value: Deported Roman captives (e.g. after Shapur I’s victories) were settled in new cities.

economicBase.value: Irrigated agriculture and Silk Road trade, with large state-managed projects.

tradeRoutes.value: Overland Silk Road and Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean trade.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver drachms. Khosrow I’s tax reform (fixed land and poll taxes).

inequality.value: A powerful nobility (great families such as Karen and Suren), Zoroastrian priests, and peasants. Mazdak’s egalitarian movement was crushed.

governmentType.value: A feudal monarchy under the “King of Kings” (shahanshah), with a centralised bureaucracy.

keyRulers.value: Ardashir I (224–241, founder). Shapur I. Shapur II (309–379). Khosrow I (531–579). Khosrow II (590–628). Yazdegerd III (632–651, last).

succession.value: Hereditary in the House of Sasan, but often disputed. After Khosrow II, many kings ruled in a few years.

institutions.value: A Zoroastrian state church, a powerful priesthood in administration, and Khosrow I’s reforms.

stability.value: Mostly strong, but with civil wars, Kavad I’s deposition (496) and the interregnum of 628–632.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between kings, the great noble houses and the priesthood.

armyAndTech.value: Heavy armoured cavalry (cataphracts), war elephants and siege warfare.

majorWars.value: Defeat of the Parthians (Hormozdgan, 224). Shapur I’s capture of the Roman emperor Valerian (Edessa, 260). The Byzantine–Sasanian War (602–628). The Arab conquest (al-Qadisiyyah 636, Nahavand 642).

territoryChange.value: About 3.5 million km² around 550 (Wikipedia infobox). Briefly held Syria, Jerusalem and Egypt (614–628).

alliancesRivals.value: Main rival: Rome and Byzantium (for four centuries). Rivals: the Hephthalites and Turks in the east, and then the Arab caliphate.

inventions.value: The Taq Kasra brick vault at Ctesiphon, and irrigation and dam works.

scienceEducation.value: The Academy of Gondishapur (medicine, science) and translations of Greek and Indian works.

openness.value: Absorbed Greek, Indian and Roman learning. Received philosophers expelled from Athens (529).

religion.value: Zoroastrianism was the official religion, with Christianity (Church of the East), Manichaeism, Judaism and Buddhism present.

artsArchitecture.value: Rock reliefs (e.g. Naqsh-e Rostam showing Valerian’s defeat), silver plates, palaces and fire temples. Its art and literature were later absorbed into Islamic culture.

socialStructure.value: Four classes (priests, warriors, scribes, commoners), with a strong nobility.

sharedIdentity.value: It called itself “Eranshahr” (Empire of the Iranians), reviving Iranian identity and Zoroastrianism.

neighbours.value: Rome and Byzantium, Armenia, Arab kingdoms, the Kushans, the Hephthalites, and India.

ideasReligions.value: Transmitted Indian and Greek knowledge, the game of chess (from India) and Persian culture to the Islamic world.

colonisation.value: Controlled Armenia, Iberia (Georgia) and parts of Arabia (e.g. Yemen, from 570s).

riseSignals.value: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians (224) and built a more centralised state.

peakPeriod.value: The reigns of Shapur I (3rd century) and Khosrow I (531–579).

declineSignals.value: The exhausting Byzantine–Sasanian War (602–628), plague, and civil strife after Khosrow II’s death.

outcome.value: Conquest. The Arab Rashidun Caliphate defeated the Sasanians (al-Qadisiyyah, Nahavand), and the last king Yazdegerd III was killed in 651.

sources.value: Royal inscriptions, coins, Roman and Byzantine histories, Arabic and Persian later sources. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Daryaee (2009).

overallCertainty.value: Good for kings and wars. Population is unknown. Some dates differ (al-Qadisiyyah 636 or 637).
